✓ProvaLivre

Personalized, anti-cheating exams for public schools with limited resources.

A teacher turns their own lecture material into a reusable question bank, then generates a different exam for every student. Same difficulty, different questions and numbers, with answer keys computed by code and checked by a human, plus step-by-step worked solutions to hand back to students.

Author: Carine Zambrano. Course: MGT 409.
GitHub: github.com/czambrano98/prova-livre
App: runs locally with python app.py, then open http://127.0.0.1:5000

1. Motivation

My uncle, Érick, teaches Mechanics of Solids at a public technical high school in Brazil, where students follow a five-year program. His school runs on limited resources, and like most public-school teachers he carries a heavy load with almost no budget for tools. His biggest assessment headache is cheating.

In his classroom, students copy from one another during exams. The practice is common enough that it has a name, "filar." One student solves a question and the answer travels down the row. Worse, because the program lasts five years and the same exam gets reused, answers get memorized and passed from one class to the next. His current options are all poor:

  • One exam for everyone, which is trivial to copy from a neighbor.
  • Hand-made variants, where he writes exercise lists with full worked solutions by hand. He described this as "trabalho da gota serena," grinding work. Making a genuinely different exam for each of 30 or 40 students, every term, for five years of students, is not feasible by hand.
"Keep a bank of, say, 50 questions. Each student's exam pulls 10 at random, so the difficulty is the same but every exam is different, so they cannot copy. For multiple choice, shuffle the answer options too. For the math questions, keep the same formula but change the input values so the answers differ. That last part is harder, I do not know how to do it."
Érick, translated from his voice messages describing what he needs.

Érick asked for one thing: a way to give every student a fair, different exam without doubling his workload. That request defined this project. The lecture material used throughout this report is his own course on plane trusses ("Treliças Planas").

2. What is new

Several tools touch pieces of this problem. None solve Érick's version of it.

Existing optionWhat it doesWhy it falls short here
LMS (Canvas, Google Classroom, Moodle)Hosts materials, collects submissionsNo exam generation, no anti-cheat question variants
Quiz tools (Google Forms, Quizizz, Kahoot)Shuffle question or option orderShuffle only. Same questions and same numbers for everyone
ChatGPTDrafts questions on requestNo saved bank, no guaranteed-correct math, no per-student assembly, no review step
Publisher test banks, ExamSoftLarge pre-built item poolsCostly, English only, generic, not from the teacher's own Portuguese material

What ProvaLivre does differently:

  1. Builds a bank from the teacher's own material, in Portuguese, tagged by concept and difficulty.
  2. Generates a unique exam per student: random selection to a chosen difficulty mix, shuffled order, shuffled multiple-choice options, and numeric questions whose numbers change for each student.
  3. For math, the model writes a parameterized template and Python computes the answer, so the answer key is always arithmetically correct. This is the part Érick said he could not figure out.
  4. A human review step. The teacher checks a worked sample before any AI-written formula reaches a student.
  5. Step-by-step worked solutions the teacher can hand to students who miss a question.
The idea that lifts this above a question generator: a code-checked numeric-variant engine, a human review step, and a cross-year guarantee that no two exams repeat, so a student in year five cannot reuse an exam from year one.

3. The agents

ProvaLivre is a short pipeline of focused agents. The first three use gpt-6-luna through Portkey, the course model and a capable, inexpensive choice. The fourth uses no model at all.

Figure 1. The agent pipeline. The first three agents (gpt-6-luna) write questions once into a saved bank. The deterministic Exam Assembler builds each student exam from that bank at no token cost. A fifth agent, the Solution Writer, adds step-by-step solutions on request (Figure 4).
AgentJobTool it usesModel
Concept ExtractorPull teachable concepts from the lecture textFile parser (PDF, PPTX, text)gpt-6-luna
Question AuthorWrite multiple-choice and short-answer questions per difficultynonegpt-6-luna
Math Variant BuilderWrite parameterized numeric templatesCode executor (checks every formula)gpt-6-luna
Exam AssemblerBuild each student exam and answer keynone (deterministic)none
Solution WriterWrite step-by-step solutions, on requestnonegpt-6-luna

The split matters. The model only writes a template and a formula, never the arithmetic. The code executor runs the formula over sample values to confirm it computes, then the Exam Assembler plugs in each student's random numbers and computes the exact answer. Language goes to the model, arithmetic goes to Python.

A real run on Érick's slides

Feeding the app his 33-page trusses lecture produced a 25-question bank in one pass:

8concepts found
25questions written
10model calls
~25swall-clock

What each agent did on that run:

Concept Extractor read the 33-page file and returned 8 concepts: plane trusses, tension and compression in members, support reactions, the method of joints, zero-force members, geometry and force decomposition, the method of sections, and global equilibrium.
Question Author wrote multiple-choice and short-answer questions. One example: "Nas hipóteses usuais de análise de uma treliça plana, onde são aplicadas as cargas e como trabalham suas barras?" Correct answer: "As cargas são aplicadas nos nós, e as barras trabalham à tração ou à compressão."
Math Variant Builder wrote a parameterized template with variables base B, height H, and load P, and the formula N = P·√((B/2)² + H²) / (2H). The code executor ran it on sample values to confirm it computes before accepting it.
Exam Assembler built one student's exam and filled that template with base 6.6 m, height 3.5 m, and load 52 kN. Python computed the axial force as 35.73 kN. The next student gets different numbers and a different answer.
Solution Writer produced the worked solution: "Pela simetria, cada membro inclinado suporta metade da carga na direção vertical. O comprimento de cada membro é √((B/2)² + H²). Igualando a componente vertical da força axial a P/2, obtém-se N = P√((B/2)² + H²)/(2H)."
Figure 2. Teacher dashboard after the real run on the trusses slides: a 25-question bank, 8 easy, 8 medium, 9 hard.
Figure 3. Generating exams: 30 students, 30 unique exams. The notice shows numeric questions held back for review.

Thirty students produced 30 unique exams, confirmed by hashing each exam's questions and options. The notice near the top shows the review step at work: numeric questions the teacher has not yet checked are held back from exams.

Printed output and worked solutions

The teacher downloads each student's exam and the answer key as PDF, with an optional school header. On request, the Solution Writer produces a commented answer key with a step-by-step solution for every question, which is what Érick wanted for students who miss a question. Solutions are written once per bank question and reused, so a whole class costs no extra tokens.

Figure 4. A student's printed exam (PDF) with the optional school header and a difficulty legend.
Figure 5. The commented answer key: each question with its correct answer and a step-by-step solution, on Érick's trusses material.

All token counts below are measured from the app's own usage log on the real trusses run. Dollar figures use a stated assumption, public GPT-4o-mini-class rates of $0.15 per 1M input and $0.60 per 1M output tokens, because the course gpt-6-luna rate is not published. Swap in the real rate and the method is unchanged.

Agent callsInputOutput
Concept Extractor (1 call, the full slide text)8,879700
Question Author (6 calls)4,0959,125
Math Variant Builder (3 calls)2,1185,225
Total (one bank build, 10 calls)15,09215,050
$0.011 to build the whole bank. Generating exams for a class, or reusing the bank for years, costs nothing more, because the Exam Assembler is deterministic and uses no model.

Cost per teacher, and at scale

The unit is a teacher. A teacher builds a bank when they start a new unit. Assume a generous two builds per month. Exams themselves are free.

ScenarioBank builds / monthMonthly cost
1 teacher2$0.023
100 teachers200$2.30
10,000 teachers20,000$226

Cost cuts, and their trade-offs

  1. Deterministic assembly, the biggest lever. A naive design would ask the model to generate each student exam. At about 16,000 tokens per exam that is roughly $0.007 per student, or $70 for a 10,000-student cohort, every exam. ProvaLivre writes once and recombines for free. Quality is unaffected, because questions are still model-written. Assembly only selects, shuffles, and fills in numbers.
  2. Batched authoring. Instead of one call per concept (about 24 calls), the app makes one call per difficulty and type across all concepts (10 calls). Measured output quality held up, as the sample questions show.
  3. Cached solutions. Worked solutions are written once per bank question, not once per student, so commented keys for a whole class cost one small generation.
  4. Input cap and a saved bank. Oversized uploads are truncated, and the bank is reused across every student and every term, so the writing cost is spread thin.

5. Safety

The app takes in untrusted files (anything a teacher uploads) and produces model output that ends up in front of students, so the risks are real: prompt injection and code injection, invented or wrong math, and runaway token spend. On top of those, the exams must never repeat across a five-year program.

Each risk has a built, tested defense. The app ships a one-click demonstration that runs them all, and every check passes.

Figure 6. The built-in safety demonstration. All eight defenses pass, including the cross-year uniqueness check.
RiskDefenseEvidence
Code injection through a formulaFormulas are parsed against a whitelist. No imports, attribute access, or arbitrary callsA system call is blocked
Prompt injection or malformed outputUntrusted material is isolated in tags, and every question is schema-checked and dropped if malformedA bad question is rejected
Invented or wrong mathThe code executor runs each formula before it is acceptedA divide-by-zero template is rejected
Unchecked AI arithmeticA human review step. AI math is held back until the teacher checks a worked sampleUnapproved math is kept off exams
OverspendingInput truncation and a hard cap on questions per buildA 150-question plan is refused
Repeat exams across yearsRandom selection, shuffled order and options, and fresh numbers per student, from a bank that grows60 exams across two terms, all unique, about 48 million question combinations before shuffling
Why the review step matters. Python computes the arithmetic perfectly, but the formula is AI-written and could be wrong. ProvaLivre never lets an unchecked formula reach a student. The teacher sees a worked example and clicks "Approve, I checked the math."

6. Impact

The headline is time and fairness, measured against how Érick works today.

30unique exams in under a minute
$0.011cost for the whole class
0repeat exams, across terms

Time. Building even a few real exam variants with worked keys by hand takes hours, and Érick does this every term. ProvaLivre produces 30 distinct exams, 30 answer keys, and a commented key with worked solutions in under a minute, from a bank that took about 25 seconds and roughly one cent to build. That saves several hours per exam cycle, repeated every unit. This is an estimate from measured generation time, pending a classroom timing.

Fairness. Copying from a neighbor stops working when the neighbor's exam has different questions, different option orders, and different numbers. Reuse across years stops working when the bank reshuffles every time. This is the "filar" problem Érick described, solved directly.

Reach. Because the cost per student is near zero, the same tool serves one classroom or a whole district for the price of a few coffees a month. Impact on a public school with limited resources counts here as much as business savings.

Real-user voice. The whole design came from Érick's own description of his needs, quoted in Section 1, and the report runs on his actual course slides. He is trying the app himself, and his reaction is below.

7. Limits and next steps

  • Question review is partly manual. Math is held behind a review step. Multiple-choice and short-answer questions are schema-checked, but their content still deserves a teacher's eye. A quick approve-and-edit flow for all types is next.
  • No student portal yet. The app is teacher-centric and export-based, with printable PDF exams, keys, and commented keys. Student logins and in-app delivery are future work.
  • Template-level approval. A teacher approves a template. Because every variant uses the same checked formula, the per-student numbers are safe once the template is approved.
  • Tested on two subjects. Built and measured on strength-of-materials and trusses material. Other subjects should work but are untested.

The whole interface switches between Portuguese and English, so Érick and an English-speaking reviewer can both use it.
